sections.title: 1. Core Study Notes
sections.content:
Detailed study guide and resources for Currency: Mansfield Commission are currently being prepared. Check back soon for comprehensive explanations, summary diagrams, and expert preparation recommendations.

Key Dimensions of Study:

  • Definition, scope, and foundational theories.
  • Relevance to General Studies Paper & Contemporary contexts.
  • Core applications and structural framework.

practiceQuestions.q: In which year was the Mansfield Commission appointed to examine the currency and coinage system in British India?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission, officially known as the Committee on Indian Coinage and Currency, was appointed in 1866 to investigate matters related to the Indian currency and mints. [Primary Reference: Standard Historical Canon - Modern India by Bipan Chandra / Spectrum]

practiceQuestions.q: Who served as the Chairman of the Mansfield Commission of 1866?
opts: Sir William Mansfield
Lord Herschell
Sir Henry Fowler
Austen Chamberlain
practiceQuestions.sol: Sir William Mansfield headed the commission appointed in 1866 to look into the state of Indian currency, specifically exploring the introduction of gold currency in India. [Primary Reference: Standard Historical Canon - Modern India History Sources]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the primary focus or term of reference for the Mansfield Commission?
opts: Inquiring into the introduction of a gold currency in British India
Establishing the Reserve Bank of India
Stopping the free coinage of silver
Fixing the Rupee-Sterling exchange rate at 1s 4d
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission was specifically appointed to examine the possibility and desirability of introducing a gold currency alongside or in place of silver in British India. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India Sources]

practiceQuestions.q: Prior to the late 19th-century currency reforms, which metal served as the principal basis of the Indian monetary standard?
opts: Gold
Silver
Bronze
Copper
practiceQuestions.sol: India was on a silver standard for the major part of the 19th century, with the silver rupee acting as the principal legal tender and standard coin. [Primary Reference: NCERT History / Economic History Canons]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following was a key recommendation made by the Mansfield Commission?
opts: Immediate adoption of a gold standard and issuance of gold coins
Issuance of gold sovereigns and legal tender status for gold coins at specified rates
Total demonetization of the silver rupee
Complete centralization of banking under the Bank of England
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission recommended the issue of gold sovereigns and half-sovereigns, and proposed making gold coins legal tender in India at fixed exchange rates, though its recommendations were not immediately implemented. [Primary Reference: Financial History of British India]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the immediate official reaction of the Government of India to the Mansfield Commission's primary recommendations?
opts: They were fully implemented within a year.
They were largely shelved or rejected due to administrative and economic concerns.
They led to the immediate creation of the Imperial Bank.
They resulted in the adoption of a bimetallic standard.
practiceQuestions.sol: Despite the Commission's report, the Government of India and the Home Government in London did not immediately implement its suggestions, as silver was still dominant and transitioning to gold posed complex financial hurdles. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India]

practiceQuestions.q: The deliberations of the Mansfield Commission highlight the 19th-century global economic shift away from which monetary system?
opts: Monometallic Silver Standard
Paper Currency Standard
Fiat Money Standard
Gold Exchange Standard
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission's focus reflected the broader 19th-century dilemma where countries relying on the silver standard faced instability due to the declining value of silver relative to gold. [Primary Reference: Modern Indian History - Economic Policies]

practiceQuestions.q: Which major event in the international commodities market during the 1870s made the issues studied by the Mansfield Commission critically important?
opts: The Great Depression of 1929
The depreciation of silver against gold globally
The discovery of massive gold reserves in South Africa
The abolition of the East India Company
practiceQuestions.sol: Although the commission met in 1866, the subsequent sharp depreciation of silver in the 1870s and 1880s vindicated the concerns about a pure silver standard, bringing currency commissions like Mansfield's into sharp historical focus. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India Sources]

practiceQuestions.q: In the context of British Indian currency history, what was the primary function of a 'Mint' during the era of the Mansfield Commission?
opts: To regulate commercial banks and set interest rates
To freely convert bullion brought by the public into standard coins
To collect land revenue on behalf of the Crown
To print paper currency notes exclusively
practiceQuestions.sol: Indian mints (such as those in Calcutta and Bombay) operated on a system of free coinage where individuals could bring silver bullion to the mint and have it coined into rupees. [Primary Reference: Financial and Economic Administration of British India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which subsequent currency committee followed the path towards altering India's silver standard by closing mints to free coinage in 1893?
opts: Herschell Commission
Hilton Young Commission
Chamberlain Commission
Fowler Committee
practiceQuestions.sol: The Herschell Commission (1893) recommended closing the Indian mints to the unrestricted coinage of silver, marking a major turning point that eventually led to the gold exchange standard. [Primary Reference: Indian Currency History - Spectrum Modern India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the economic and administrative rationale behind the Mansfield Commission reflect the broader challenges of 'Home Charges' for British India?
opts: Fluctuations in silver value made remittances to Britain in gold (Home Charges) highly unpredictable and costly.
Home charges could only be paid through gold bullion, necessitating a strict gold standard.
The Mansfield Commission was formed specifically to eliminate home charges altogether.
Home charges required the immediate abolition of paper currency in India.
None of the above
practiceQuestions.sol: The Government of India had to remit substantial sums to London (Home Charges) in gold or sterling. When the silver rupee depreciated against sterling, the cost of making these remittances skyrocketed, forcing commissions like Mansfield's to explore alternative monetary bases. [Primary Reference: Economic History of British India - Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the structural dilemma faced by the colonial economy in the 1860s regarding the choice between a silver standard and a gold standard?
opts: Silver suited internal trade and traditional taxation, while international trade with Britain favored gold linkages.
Gold was too abundant in India, causing severe hyperinflation.
Indians refused to accept silver coins entirely.
The British Parliament banned the use of silver throughout the British Empire.
practiceQuestions.sol: While India's internal economy and Asian trade were deeply entrenched in silver, Britain and Western Europe operated on the gold standard. This divergence created deep structural friction, prompting investigations by bodies like the Mansfield Commission. [Primary Reference: Cambridge Economic History of India, Vol. 2]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the Mansfield Commission's proposal to introduce gold coins face practical implementation difficulties in the mid-19th century?
opts: Gold was globally undervalued, and silver was universally preferred by all European powers.
Gold was scarce globally, and pegging the silver rupee to a gold standard would have required massive gold reserves that India lacked.
The Indian population aggressively hoarded silver and destroyed all gold artifacts.
The East India Company opposed any form of metallic currency.
practiceQuestions.sol: Introducing a gold standard or gold currency required substantial gold backing at a time when gold supplies were relatively tight and Britain itself was protective of its gold reserves. Transitioning a massive silver-based economy like India posed immense logistical and financial risks. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India - T.R. Jain / Dutt]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the recommendations of the Mansfield Commission contrast with the later policy implemented by the Herschell Commission in 1893?
opts: Mansfield explored introducing gold alongside silver, whereas Herschell recommended closing silver mints to create artificial scarcity of silver rupees.
Mansfield wanted to ban paper currency, while Herschell expanded it.
Mansfield recommended a bimetallic standard, while Herschell completely ignored metallic money.
There was no difference; both advocated identical measures.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission (1866) looked at adding gold to the currency mix when silver was still stable. By 1893, the severe collapse of silver forced the Herschell Commission to take the drastic step of closing mints to free coinage, shifting the focus from adding gold to manipulating the silver rupee's exchange value. [Primary Reference: Indian Financial History - Official Archives]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the significance of the 'Sovereign' in the discussions surrounding the Mansfield Commission?
opts: It was proposed as a British gold coin to circulate concurrently with the Indian silver rupee.
It was the title given to the Governor-General of India for monetary affairs.
It referred to the supreme authority of the Bank of England over Indian mints.
It was a paper bond issued to pay off India's national debt.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission deliberated on authorizing the British gold sovereign (and half-sovereign) to circulate in India as legal tender at a fixed ratio with the rupee, representing an early attempt to bridge the gold-silver divide. [Primary Reference: Numismatic and Financial History of British India]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the colonial administration fear the unmanaged influx of silver into Indian mints during the late 19th century?
opts: It threatened to flood the market, cheapen the rupee excessively, and disrupt budgetary calculations.
It would cause gold to completely disappear from British reserves.
It made paper currency completely redundant.
It violated international treaties signed with the United States.
practiceQuestions.sol: Under the system of free coinage, anyone could bring silver to the mints. As world silver production surged and its price fell, unlimited silver coinage meant the rupee's exchange value plummeted, severely impacting the colonial government's ability to pay sterling obligations. Committees like Mansfield's and later Herschell's grappled with this systemic vulnerability. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India - Dutt / Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q: In what way did the evolution of Indian currency commissions (from Mansfield in 1866 to Hilton Young in 1926) reflect India's integration into the global capitalist economy?
opts: They showed a progressive shift from localized silver independence to absolute subordination to international gold standards and imperial financial control.
They demonstrated India's complete isolation from global monetary trends.
They highlighted India's dominance over the Bank of England.
They proved that India operated an independent fiat currency system unaffected by external markets.
practiceQuestions.sol: The progression of currency committees mirrors the tightening web of imperial finance. From exploring gold integration in 1866 (Mansfield) to establishing the Reserve Bank and gold-pegged standards later, Indian monetary policy was continually restructured to serve imperial remittance needs and global trade stability. [Primary Reference: Modern Indian History - Economic Imperialism Canons]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the core argument presented by proponents of a gold standard for India during the deliberations of the 19th-century currency commissions?
opts: It would attract foreign capital, stabilize exchange rates, and protect savings from the depreciation of silver.
It would abolish all taxes levied on Indian peasants.
It would allow India to mint unlimited copper coins.
It would immediately transfer political independence to Indian nationalists.
practiceQuestions.sol: Advocates of the gold standard argued that silver was too volatile. A gold standard would align India with Britain, attract British investment by removing exchange risk, and halt the continuous decline in the real value of savings held in rupees. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India - Dadabhai Naoroji / R.C. Dutt context]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did the British Treasury and the India Office often resist recommendations for a full gold standard in India despite inquiries like Mansfield's?
opts: Fear that a massive drain of gold to India would deplete London's reserves and disrupt the international gold market.
They believed India was too wealthy and did not need financial reform.
They wanted India to adopt a purely barter-based economy.
The Governor-General of India legally prohibited the import of gold.
practiceQuestions.sol: Imperial authorities were haunted by the prospect that if India were permitted to freely draw gold into its monetary system (given India's historical propensity to absorb precious metals), it would drain London's gold reserves and threaten the global supremacy of the pound sterling. [Primary Reference: Imperial Finance and the India Office Archives]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the Mansfield Commission's investigation into currency set a precedent for future colonial economic governance in India?
opts: It established the practice of appointing expert parliamentary/official commissions to diagnose structural monetary crises before enacting sweeping changes.
It proved that commissions were useless and should never be formed.
It directly empowered Indian elected representatives to control monetary policy.
It mandated that all future currency must be printed in local Indian languages.
None of the above
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mansfield Commission was among the earliest formal expert bodies set up by the British administration to methodically investigate complex currency dilemmas in India, paving the way for subsequent high-profile committees like Herschell, Fowler, Chamberlain, and Hilton Young. [Primary Reference: Institutional History of British India Administration]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Mansfield Commission:
1. It was appointed in the year 1866 under the chairmanship of Sir William Mansfield.
2. Its primary mandate was to inquire into the feasibility of introducing a gold currency in British India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Mansfield Commission was indeed appointed in 1866, chaired by Sir William Mansfield, commander-in-chief of the Bombay army (later commander-in-chief in India), specifically to examine the introduction of gold coins/currency in British India alongside or supplementing the silver standard. [Primary Reference: Historical Archives on Indian Currency Commissions]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the monetary condition of British India during the 1860s:
1. India was predominantly on a silver standard with the silver rupee serving as the principal standard coin.
2. Indian mints were closed to the free coinage of silver during the tenure of the Mansfield Commission.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: India was on a silver standard in the 1860s, and the silver rupee was the chief legal tender. Statement 2 is incorrect: Indian mints were *not* closed to the free coinage of silver in 1866; they practiced open, free coinage of silver. Mints were only closed much later, in 1893, upon the recommendation of the Herschell Commission. [Primary Reference: Economic History of India - Bipan Chandra / Spectrum]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the recommendations of the Mansfield Commission:
1. It recommended that the British gold sovereign and half-sovereign should be made legal tender in India at specified rates.
2. It advocated for the immediate and total abolition of the silver rupee to establish a pure gold standard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The Mansfield Commission recommended the authorization of gold sovereigns and half-sovereigns as legal tender at fixed exchange rates with the rupee. Statement 2 is incorrect: It did *not* recommend abolishing the silver rupee; rather, it proposed introducing gold concurrently alongside or to supplement the existing silver currency, not immediate total demonetization. [Primary Reference: Financial Records of British India Currency Committees]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the impact of silver depreciation on British India:
1. The depreciation of silver against gold in the late 19th century increased the rupee cost of meeting sterling obligations ('Home Charges').
2. The Mansfield Commission was the direct result of the currency crisis caused by the 1893 closure of mints.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: As silver depreciated, the colonial government had to pay more rupees to purchase the same amount of sterling to meet Home Charges in London. Statement 2 is incorrect: Chronologically, the Mansfield Commission met in 1866, long *before* the 1893 closure of mints (which was recommended by the Herschell Commission). [Primary Reference: Economic History of India - Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding colonial currency commissions in India:
1. The Mansfield Commission (1866) and the Herschell Commission (1893) both dealt with problems arising from the metallic standard of Indian currency.
2. Both commissions immediately succeeded in establishing a full gold standard in India without any friction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Both commissions were established to address severe structural challenges related to the silver/metallic standard in India. Statement 2 is incorrect: Neither commission immediately established a full gold standard; their recommendations faced severe bureaucratic hesitation, delay, and incremental policy shifts rather than instant success. [Primary Reference: Cambridge Economic History of India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of mints in 19th-century British India:
1. The mints in Calcutta and Bombay accepted silver from private merchants and citizens and coined it into rupees free of charge other than a nominal seigniorage.
2. The Mansfield Commission examined how the operations of these mints interacted with proposals for introducing gold currency.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Indian mints operated on an open, free coinage system for silver until 1893. The Mansfield Commission (1866) evaluated the functioning of these mints and how introducing gold alongside or within the mint framework would affect monetary stability. [Primary Reference: Economic and Monetary History of India Archives]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the global monetary context in the 1860s:
1. Most major Western economies were rapidly moving towards or consolidating a gold standard during this period.
2. British India was under economic pressure to maintain complete isolation from international precious metal price trends.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: The mid-to-late 19th century witnessed the ascendancy of the gold standard in Britain, Europe, and the US. Statement 2 is incorrect: British India was *not* isolated; rather, its heavy financial ties to Britain made it intensely vulnerable to international silver depreciation and gold price movements, which is precisely why commissions like Mansfield's were formed. [Primary Reference: Global Monetary History - Eichengreen / Cambridge History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the outcomes and legacy of the Mansfield Commission:
1. Its recommendations were immediately enacted into law by Viceroy Lord Lawrence, creating the first Indian gold reserve.
2. Although its specific proposals were not immediately operationalized, it initiated official colonial discourse on altering India's single-metal silver standard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect: Lord Lawrence's administration and the Home Government did not immediately enact the Mansfield Commission's recommendations into law, and no immediate gold reserve was created from it. Statement 2 is correct: The commission's primary legacy lies in establishing the first formal official investigation into gold currency adoption, laying the groundwork for subsequent 19th- and early 20th-century currency reforms. [Primary Reference: Administrative History of British India Canons]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic arguments concerning Indian currency in the 19th century:
1. Indian nationalists like Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt frequently analyzed how currency manipulations and exchange rate losses harmed Indian taxpayers.
2. The Mansfield Commission was established as a direct representative body of the Indian National Congress to protect indigenous commerce.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct: Early nationalist economists critiqued colonial financial policies, including exchange rate losses imposed on Indian revenues. Statement 2 is incorrect: The Mansfield Commission was set up in 1866 by the British colonial government, whereas the Indian National Congress was not founded until 1885. It had no representation from or relation to the INC. [Primary Reference: Economic Critique of Nationalism - Bipan Chandra]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the trajectory of Indian currency committees from 1866 to 1926:
1. The Mansfield Commission (1866) was the starting point of official government inquiries into integrating gold into the Indian monetary system.
2. The Hilton Young Commission (1926), decades later, ultimately recommended the establishment of a central bank (Reserve Bank of India) and the adoption of the gold bullion/exchange standard.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. The Mansfield Commission (1866) marked the earliest formal inquiry into gold currency for India. Decades later, following committees like Herschell, Fowler, and Chamberlain, the Hilton Young Commission (1926) culminated in the blueprint for the Reserve Bank of India and structural monetary modernization. [Primary Reference: RBI Official History & Indian Financial Evolution Canons]
